Abstract 23 
Background: Nonsense variants in CFTR account for ~10% of cystic fibrosis (CF) variants 24 
and cannot be treated with approved CFTR modulators. Translational readthrough agents such 25 
as ELX-02 offer a potential therapeutic strategy, but clinical trials evaluated mainly in G542X 26 
CFTR nonsense variant and underlined limited efficacy. This study aimed to evaluate ELX-27 
02-mediated CFTR rescue across a broad range of nonsense variants using patient-derived 28 
intestinal organoids (PDIOs) to define variant-specific determinants of readthrough efficacy 29 
and assess its potential across a genetically diverse CF population. 30 
Method: The ex vivo response to ELX-02 was assessed in 206 PDIOs carrying heterogeneous 31 
nonsense variants. CFTR function was quantified using forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) 32 
assay after 48-hour exposure to ELX-02. Responses were analysed by genotype and stop 33 
codon identity, with secondary validation performed in a selected subset of PDIOs (n = 60). 34 
Results: ELX-02–mediated CFTR rescue varied markedly, ranging from responses 35 
approaching those observed with approved CFTR modulators (LUM/IVA) to responses at or 36 
below detection limit. Overall, maximal responses were modest and at the lower end of the 37 
functional range for CFTR modulators. Rescue was dose-dependent and higher in PDIOs 38 
carrying two nonsense variants when compared with PDIOs carrying a single nonsense 39 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission.

variant combined with a residual or minimal function variant. Nonsense variants in 40 
nucleotide-binding domain 1, including G542X, S466X, G550X and R553X, showed 41 
relatively higher responsiveness.  42 
Conclusion: ELX-02 induces limited and highly heterogeneous CFTR rescue across nonsense 43 
variants. PDIO-based functional screening provides a framework to guide patient selection 44 
and stratification for future readthrough therapy trials. 45 
Keywords 46 
Premature termination codon; Readthrough therapy; ELX-02, Patient-derived intestinal 47 
organoids, Forskolin-induced swelling assay  48 
Introduction 49 
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a life-limiting autosomal recessive disorder caused by variants in the 50 
CFTR gene, resulting in defective chloride and bicarbonate transport and progressive 51 
multiorgan disease, particularly affecting the lungs and gastrointestinal tract (1). Among the 52 
more than 2000 described CFTR variants, nonsense variants introduce premature termination 53 
codons (PTCs), which lead to truncated, non-functional proteins and often trigger degradation 54 
of the corresponding mRNAs via nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD) (2-4). Nonsense 55 
variants account for 8.4% of all CF-causing CFTR alleles worldwide 56 
(http://www.genet.sickkids.on.ca/). The subset of people with CF (pwCF) homozygous for a 57 
nonsense variant or in trans with another class I variant are ineligible for currently approved 58 
CFTR modulators, which primarily target gating or processing defects of the protein. 59 
One promising therapeutic approach for this underserved population involves translational 60 
readthrough agents (5). These compounds act by modulating ribosomal fidelity at the PTC 61 
site, enabling the incorporation of amino acids (AA) at the site of the PTC and allowing 62 
translation to continue to the normal termination codon (NTC), ultimately producing full-63 
length CFTR protein. Mechanistically, different classes of readthrough agents can act through 64 
distinct pathways. Aminoglycosides, for example, transiently slow ribosomal translocation 65 
and promote mispairing at the nonsense site, whereas more recent compounds, such as di-2,6-66 
aminopurine (DAP), target tRNA-modifying enzymes to facilitate the selective incorporation 67 
of cognate AA at the nonsense site (6-9). In all cases, readthrough efficacy is influenced by 68 
the identity of the stop codon, the surrounding nucleotide context, and the location of the 69 
nonsense within the transcript (10). 70 
Despite their promise, no readthrough agent has yet demonstrated clinical efficacy for pwCF. 71 
Ataluren, the furthest developed for Duchenne muscular dystrophy, failed to show robust 72 
improvement in large scale CF clinical trials (11, 12). Similarly, ELX-02, a chemically 73 
engineered aminoglycoside that reached the furthest stage in CF-specific clinical 74 
development, has so far only been tested in a small cohort of patients carrying the G542X 75 
variant, either alone or in combination with the CFTR potentiator ivacaftor. Phase 2 trials 76 
revealed limited functional and clinical benefit, which may at least partially be explained by 77 
suboptimal pharmacodynamic properties, including low pulmonary drug concentrations (6, 78 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission. 
The copyright holder for this preprintthis version posted August 3, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.31.740556doi: bioRxiv preprint 
3 
 
13). These translational gaps underscore the challenges of developing readthrough therapies 79 
and highlight the need for a deeper mechanistic understanding and broader preclinical 80 
evaluation. 81 
Patient-derived intestinal organoids (PDIOs) represent a powerful platform to bridge this 82 
translational gap. PDIOs are three-dimensional cultures derived from adult stem cells isolated 83 
from intestinal crypts, which recapitulate key features of the native epithelium, including cell 84 
polarity, cell-type composition, and CFTR expression predominantly at the apical membrane 85 
(14-16). Forskolin-induced swelling (FIS) of PDIOs provides a quantitative readout of CFTR-86 
dependent fluid secretion, which correlates with clinical disease severity, progression, and 87 
response to modulators (17, 18). As a result, PDIOs enable patient-specific and variant-88 
specific preclinical assessment of therapeutic strategies, including readthrough compounds, 89 
under physiologically relevant conditions (19, 20). Moreover, PDIOs can be expanded and 90 
cryopreserved to create living biobanks that represent a wide spectrum of CFTR genotypes, 91 
facilitating systematic evaluation of novel therapies (21, 22). 92 
Here, we used PDIOs to systematically evaluate the ex vivo response to ELX-02 across a 93 
broad set of CFTR nonsense variants. By expanding beyond the single G542X genotype 94 
previously tested in clinical trials, we aimed to define variant-specific determinants of 95 
readthrough efficacy and assess the potential of ELX-02 to rescue CFTR function across a 96 
genetically diverse CF population. This study provides a comprehensive preclinical 97 
framework to guide future development of readthrough therapies and improve patient 98 
stratification for clinical trials. 99 
Materials and Methods 100 
PDIO Culture and Expansion 101 
Within the HIT-CF project, 489 PDIOs from PwCF in 12 countries were collected in a central 102 
biobank (23) for the HIT-CF Organoid Study (NTR7520). All participating clinical sites were 103 
members of the clinical trial network of the European Cystic Fibrosis Society (ECFS-CTN). 104 
This study and the accompanying informed consent form were approved by independent 105 
ethics committees at each participating site, with final approval for use of all PDIOs by TcBio 106 
(24-263). Written informed consent was obtained from each participant and/or the 107 
participant's legal guardian. 108 
PDIOs from patients carrying at least one CFTR nonsense variant were selected for the 109 
present analysis. The selected samples were divided between the three European labs 110 
participating in the HIT-CF European project (KULeuven, ULisboa and UMC Utrecht). 111 
PDIOs were thawed and seeded in a 24-well plate with medium supplemented with Rho-112 
associated kinase inhibitor (RhoKI) according to the previously published Standard Operating 113 
Procedure (SOP) (15). Cultures were maintained at 37°C with 5% CO 2 and passaged weekly 114 
to promote growth and budding. PDIO quality and morphology were monitored, and after at 115 
least 3 weeks of expansion, cultures were used to perform the FIS assay. 116 
Forskolin induced swelling assay 117 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission. 
The copyright holder for this preprintthis version posted August 3, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.31.740556doi: bioRxiv preprint 
4 
 
PDIO cultures were split mechanically every 7 days and after disruption replated at a density 118 
of 20-50 PDIOs per 4 µL droplet in a 96-well plate, as previously described (15). Plates were 119 
incubated at 37°C with 5% CO 2 for a maximum of 10 minutes before adding the respective 120 
compound solutions. For each PDIO sample, two screens were performed, with each 121 
experiment repeated in duplicate with two technical replicates. In the primary screen, media-122 
only controls were compared to 80 µM ELX-02 and 160 µM ELX-02. In the secondary 123 
screen, media-only controls were compared to 40 µM ELX-02, and 80 µM ELX-02. 124 
After a 48-hour incubation period with or without ELX-02, PDIOs were stained with calcein 125 
AM for 15-20 minutes to visually assess viability. Following the viability assessment, PDIOs 126 
swelling was measured using the FIS assay. PDIOs swelling was stimulated by adding 127 
forskolin at a single final concentration of 0.8 µM (no titration). Images were captured every 128 
20 minutes for 120 minutes on a confocal microscope, yielding seven timepoints for analysis. 129 
Total organoid area was calculated from the captured images by integrated imaging analysis 130 
software (Zen from Zeiss). The raw area data for each timepoint and well were used to 131 
calculate the Area Under the Curve (AUC) for normalized swelling over the 120-minute 132 
experiment duration. To normalize for differences associated with sites, we characterized 133 
ELX-02 mediated swelling of the same G542X/G542X PDIO line at the 3 sites; calculated the 134 
mean and normalized all FIS data for the differences of this median at ELX-02 at a 135 
concentration of 80 µM. The mean ELX-02 mediated swelling of the G542X/G542X lines 136 
were used as a reference line throughout the figures.  137 
Final dataset and study design 138 
From the HIT-CF biobank, all PDIOs carrying at least one nonsense variant (n = 223) were 139 
included in the initial selection for the primary screen. A total of 17 samples were excluded 140 
afterwards for the following reasons: reference samples (G542X/G542X) (n = 6), ≥  1 141 
unknown variant (n = 6), equivocal nonsense variants (G587X/G587X, R347X/R347X) (n = 142 
2), less than 2 CF causing variants (M470V/Q1313X, M470V/W1282X) (n = 2), no nonsense 143 
variant (n = 1). After these exclusions, results from 206 PDIOs were available and included in 144 
the primary screen.  145 
Based on the results in the primary screen, the highest responders were selected for a 146 
subsequent validation screen (secondary screen). In total, 60 PDIOs were re-tested by HUB 147 
Organoids: 57 PDIOs identified as top responders and 3 classified as non-responders for 148 
negative control. Selection was stratified across three batches, corresponding to the three 149 
participating screening laboratories. Sample selection for validation screen was performed by 150 
a statistician at UMCU, who was blinded to genotype. Three additional criteria were applied: 151 
1) exclusion of PDIOs allocated to the CHOICES clinical trial (part of the HIT-CF project) 152 
evaluating diponecaftor (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT064685270; EudraCT 2022-500410-26-01); 153 
2) exclusion of PDIOs with high residual CFTR function (>2500 AUC after forskolin only), 154 
as these display limited additional drug-induced swelling; 3) inclusion of the highest 25% of 155 
ELX-02 responders at 80 µM (residual function-corrected) at each site. 156 
Statistics 157 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission. 
The copyright holder for this preprintthis version posted August 3, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.31.740556doi: bioRxiv preprint 
5 
 
To evaluate the functional response of each PDIO line to the tested compound solutions, area 158 
under the curve (AUC) values were calculated using “R” software. To correct for residual 159 
function (swelling induced by forskolin alone indicating partly functional CFTR), the 160 
medium-only control was used in which swelling was measured with the presence of forskolin 161 
but in the absence of ELX-02.  162 
All subsequent statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 30.0.0, 163 
IBM). Group comparisons were conducted using Kruskal–Wallis tests, followed by 164 
Bonferroni-corrected Mann–Whitney U tests for pairwise comparisons, as most variables 165 
were not normally distributed. Paired responses across different ELX-02 concentrations were 166 
compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Correlations were assessed using the 167 
Spearman correlation coefficient. Enrichment of individual PTC variants among top-168 
responding PDIOs was evaluated using 2×2 contingency tables, with odds ratios (ORs) and 169 
95% confidence intervals calculated; significance was determined by Pearson Chi-square or 170 
Fisher’s Exact Test for small expected counts (cells <5), based on observed counts. All tests 171 
were two-sided, with statistical significance set at 0.05. No prior power analysis was 172 
performed. Graphs were made using GraphPad Prism (version 10.6.1). 173 
Results 174 
Study and subject overview 175 
In the primary screen, PDIOs from 206 subjects carrying at least one nonsense variant were 176 
included. A full overview of the study design is provided in Figure 1A. Across this cohort, 48 177 
distinct nonsense variants were analysed. Their positions within the CFTR mRNA are shown 178 
in Figure 1B, underlining the inclusion of nonsense variants throughout the whole CFTR 179 
gene. 180 
All variants reported in this study were classified into three categories: 1) nonsense variants, 181 
2) minimal function (MF) variants, 3) other variants. Classification proceeded as follows: first 182 
all the nonsense variants according to the CFTR1 database nomenclature were assigned to the 183 
nonsense category (http://www.genet.sickkids.on.ca/). Next, all remaining (non-nonsense) 184 
variants were categorized according to the VX-445/TEZ/IV A eligibility list: variants 185 
designated as minimal-function in this document were classified as MF (24), and all others 186 
were categorized as “other”. An overview of this classification is provided in Figure 1C . 187 
Based on these criteria, PDIOs were grouped into three genotype categories: 188 
nonsense/nonsense (n = 62), nonsense/MF (n = 82), and nonsense/other (n = 62). Residual 189 
CFTR function was assessed by FIS over 2 hours in the absence of ELX-02 as shown for each 190 
PDIO in Figure 1D . Within the nonsense/MF group, one PDIO with genotype 191 
G542X/R1066C displayed unexpectedly high residual function, representing a notable outlier. 192 
Residual CFTR function differed significantly across the three genotype groups (H = 74.06, df 193 
= 2, p < 0.001). No difference was observed between the nonsense/nonsense and 194 
nonsense/MF groups, whereas the nonsense/other group exhibited higher residual function 195 
than both the nonsense/nonsense and nonsense/MF groups, as shown in Figure 1E. 196 
Genotype-dependent response to ELX-02 in PDIOs primary screen 197 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission.

We next set out to compare genotype-dependent responses to ELX-02. Figure 2A and 2B 198 
show the residual function-corrected 0.8 µM FIS response to ELX-02 at 80 µM in PDIOs 199 
belonging to the nonsense/nonsense and nonsense/MF genotype groups, respectively. Only 200 
PDIOs with a response above 1384 AUC are shown, corresponding to the benchmark of the 201 
mean response to ELX-02 at 80 µM in G542X-homozygous PDIOs. Responses below this 202 
benchmark are considered not clinically relevant and are not shown in the figure. The residual 203 
function-corrected 0.8 µM FIS response to ELX-02 at 80 µM in PDIOs belonging to the 204 
nonsense/other genotype group is shown in Figure S2.  205 
Within the nonsense/nonsense group (n = 62), one PDIO exhibited a response exceeding the 206 
mean response to elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaf tor (ETI) in F508del-h omozygous PDIOs, and 207 
eight PDIOs showed responses exceeding the mean LUM/IV A response benchmark. Thirty-208 
eight PDIOs exceeded the mean response to ELX-02 in G542X-homozygous PDIOs as shown 209 
in Figure 2A. In the nonsense/MF group (n = 77), three PDIOs demonstrated mean responses 210 
above the mean LUM/IV A benchmark and thirty PDIOs showed responses exceeding mean 211 
ELX-02 response in G542X-homozygous PDIOs, as shown in Figure 2B.  212 
Inspection of individual responses revealed that the two highest-responding PDIOs both 213 
carried the S466X variant, with the S466X/G542X genotype showing a response comparable 214 
to the mean ETI response observed in F508del-homozygous PDIOs.  215 
Among the top 10% responders, three nonsense variants, S466X, G542X and Q525X, showed 216 
enrichment (S466X: OR 1.11, 95% CI 0.96 – 1.27, p = 0.010; G542X: OR 4.54, 95% CI 217 
1.79–11.51, p < 0.001; Q525X: OR 1.17, 95% CI 0.98 – 1.39, p < 0.001), whereas other 218 
nonsense variants, including G550X, R553X and E585X, were also observed among the top 219 
10% responders but were not enriched. Interestingly, all these nonsense variants were located 220 
within the NBD1 domain. In contrast, PDIOs harboring W1282X were underrepresented 221 
among the top 10% responders (OR 0.14, 95% CI 0.018 – 1.06, p = 0.030) indicating that this 222 
variant is associated with lower ELX-02 responsiveness.  223 
Swelling upon ELX-02 at 80 µM differed significantly across the three genotype categories 224 
(Figure 2C). The residual function-corrected FIS responses to ELX-02 at 80 µM were highest 225 
in PDIOs carrying two nonsense variants, compared with PDIOs carrying one nonsense and 226 
one MF variant. Both the nonsense/nonsense and nonsense/MF groups showed significantly 227 
higher residual function-corrected FIS responses than the nonsense/other group ( Figure 2C). 228 
Using ELX-02 at 160 µM, similar responses in both the nonsense/nonsense and nonsense/MF 229 
were found compared to the response to ELX-02 at 80 µM. However, in PDIOs with 230 
nonsense/other genotype, ELX-02 at 160 µM concentration reduced FIS responses compared 231 
to 80 µM ( Figure 2C). Negative FIS values indicate that FIS after exposure to ELX-02 was 232 
lower than residual function. At 160 µM ELX-02, more negative responses were observed. 233 
Organoid morphology in PDIOs with high residual function and subsequent reduced swelling 234 
upon adding ELX-02 is shown in Figure S1.  235 
Although some of the PDIOs harbor identical genotypes, the majority carry unique 236 
compound-heterozygous genotypes. Therefore, our study has a theratyping character rather 237 
th
an a genotyping approach. In Figure 2D, the violin plots of genotypes with at least two 238

available PDIOs reveal higher variability for G542X/R1066C and I1234V/W1282X, whereas 239 
genotypes such as Q525X/3732delA, G85E/G542X and 1717-1G>A/W1088X show minimal 240 
variability. ELX-02 responses at 80 /i2 µM did not differ between PDIOs with nonsenses close 241 
to the downstream exon–intron junction ( ≤ 55/i2 nt) and those further away (>55 /i2 nt), 242 
suggesting that downstream junction distance alone does not predict readthrough efficacy 243 
(Mann-Whitney U = 3545, p = 0.075). 244 
Finally, responses were analyzed according to the type of nonsense codon in PDIOs carrying 245 
either two nonsense variants with the same nonsense codon or one nonsense variant and one 246 
MF variant. Most nonsense variants introduced a TGA stop codon (n = 102), compared with 247 
TAA (n = 20) and TAG (n = 11). While residual function did not differ between nonsense 248 
categories, ELX-02-induced responses at both 80 µM and 160 µM were significantly lower in 249 
PDIOs harboring TAA nonsense codons than in those with TAG and TGA (Figure 2E). 250 
Validation of genotype-dependent differential responses to ELX-02  251 
In the secondary screen, 57 PDIOs with the highest response and 3 PDIOs with no response as 252 
control were selected, including 31 nonsense/nonsense, 21 nonsense/MF and 8 nonsense/other 253 
PDIOs, and re-screened at a different institute (HUB). ELX-02 was tested at lower 254 
concentrations (40 µM and 80 µM) than in the primary screen, reflecting clinically relevant 255 
ELX-02 plasma levels (6, 25). 256 
Residual function and residual function-corrected FIS responses to ELX-02 at 80 µM and at 257 
40 µM did not differ significantly across the three genotype groups ( Figure S3). Figures 3A 258 
and 3B show the individual responses to ELX-02 at 80 µM and at 40 µM for 259 
nonsense/nonsense and nonsense/MF, respectively. Residual function-corrected FIS responses 260 
to ELX-02 at 80 µM were significantly higher than at 40 µM (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 261 
0.001). Figure 3C illustrates intragenotype variation for genotypes with two or more PDIOs. 262 
Responses were relatively consistent for R1162X/N1303K, W1282X/W1282X, and 263 
G542X/E585X, whereas responses in G542X/R553X were more heterogeneous, indicating 264 
higher intragenotype variability in this case. 265 
Overall individual response patterns were comparable between primary and secondary screen, 266 
such as S466X-containing genotypes consistently ranking among highest responders whereas 267 
PDIOs carrying W1282X variants again clustered among the lower responders. A comparison 268 
between results from the primary screen to the secondary screen are shown in Figure S4. 269 
Discussion 270 
We describe FIS responses to the readthrough agent ELX-02 in a large cohort of PDIOs from 271 
people with CF harboring a broad range of nonsense variants, extending prior PDIO studies 272 
focused mostly on G542X, for which ELX-02 failed to demonstrate clinical benefit (6, 8, 13). 273 
Responses to ELX-02 varied markedly between subjects, ranging from effects that 274 
approached those observed in F508del/F508del PDIOs treated with LUM/IV A, to minimal 275 
responses. Overall, maximal FIS responses were modest and remained at the lower end of the 276 
range observed for approved CFTR modulators, consistent with the limited clinical efficacy 277 
reported for ELX-02 to date (6, 13). These findings indicate that ELX-02 monotherapy is 278 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission. 
The copyright holder for this preprintthis version posted August 3, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.31.740556doi: bioRxiv preprint 
8 
 
likely insufficient for robust functional rescue, underscoring the need to better understand the 279 
determinants of readthrough efficacy and to develop more effective strategies. 280 
PDIO responses to ELX-02 were dose-dependent and higher in PDIOs carrying two nonsense 281 
variants compared with those carrying a single nonsense variant in combination with a 282 
residual or minimal function allele, as expected based on target availability. Among individual 283 
genotypes, G542X PDIOs consistently showed higher responses than most other nonsense 284 
variants. Elevated responses were also observed for S466X, G550X and R553X, which are 285 
notably all located within NBD1. However, responsiveness was not dependent on the distance 286 
of the nonsense variant to the nearest intron or the canonical ±55 base pair region associated 287 
with nonsense-mediated decay (26), although it should be noted that we did not directly 288 
quantify mutant transcript abundance (e.g., by qPCR), and therefore cannot fully exclude a 289 
contribution of NMD-mediated reduction of mutant CFTR mRNA to the variability in ELX-290 
02 responsiveness observed across variants. One possible explanation for the higher 291 
responsiveness observed among several NBD1-located variants is that amino acid 292 
substitutions generated during readthrough are better tolerated at specific NBD1 residues. 293 
Notably, variants such as S466X are located outside the canonical A TP-binding and catalytic 294 
motifs of NBD1, suggesting that successful readthrough may generate full-length CFTR 295 
proteins that retain substantial function despite incorporation of a non-native amino acid. 296 
Consequently, nonsense variants at these positions may be less sensitive to the identity of the 297 
incorporated amino acid, although local sequence context surrounding the PTC may also 298 
contribute, as has been suggested in the context of tRNA-based suppression therapies and 299 
may similarly apply to readthrough approaches (27). More likely, however, responsiveness is 300 
determined by the functional properties of the resulting readthrough-derived missense CFTR 301 
protein. This concept is exemplified by G550X, for which the putative readthrough product 302 
G550W has been shown to generate a highly functional CFTR protein (28). Stratification by 303 
stop codon identity revealed higher median responses for TGA codons, the most frequent stop 304 
codon in CFTR, and lower responses for TAA codons. This is consistent with previous 305 
findings demonstrating that translation termination fidelity and readthrough efficiency 306 
depend, among other factors, on stop codon identity, with termination efficiency ranked as 307 
TAA > TAG > TGA and corresponding readthrough efficiency as TGA > TAG > TAA (29). 308 
Nonetheless, this association was not absolute, as exemplified by the TAA variant Q525X, 309 
which was among the strongest responders. Thus, neither stop codon identity nor nonsense 310 
position alone appears sufficient to predict readthrough efficacy. Instead, responsiveness 311 
likely reflects the combined effects of transcript availability, local sequence context, 312 
readthrough efficiency, and the functional consequences of the amino acid incorporated 313 
during readthrough (30). Future studies combining quantitative proteomics allowing 314 
identification of incorporated amino acids, and functional assessment of corresponding 315 
missense variants may help disentangle the relative contribution of these mechanisms. 316 
Despite the identification of responsive genotypes, the overall magnitude of rescue remained 317 
limited. To interpret these responses in a clinical context, three benchmarks can be considered. 318 
The lowest benchmark is the mean ELX-02-induced FIS response in G542X/G542X PDIOs, 319 
since clinical trials with ELX-02 failed to demonstrate clinically meaningful improvements in 320 
lung function or biomarkers, either as monotherapy or in combination with a potentiator (6, 321 
(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission. 
The copyright holder for this preprintthis version posted August 3, 2026. ; https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.31.740556doi: bioRxiv preprint 
9 
 
13). PDIOs response falling below this threshold are therefore unlikely to confer any clinical 322 
benefit. The intermediate benchmark is the LUM/IV A-induced FIS response in 323 
F508del/F508del PDIOs, a modulator that demonstrated only modest improvements in FEV/i2  324 
of approximately three percent predicted in clinical trials, detectable only in large patient 325 
cohorts (31). PDIOs with responses between the ELX-02 and LUM/IV A benchmarks thus 326 
represent a zone of uncertain clinical relevance. The highest benchmark is the ETI-induced 327 
FIS response in F508del/F508del PDIOs, which corresponds to robust clinical benefit. PDIOs 328 
exceeding this threshold are therefore most likely to show a meaningful clinical response. The 329 
relatively low range of ELX-02–mediated rescue in PDIOs therefore provides a plausible 330 
explanation for the absence of clear clinical benefit observed thus far. Although ELX-02 was 331 
assessed as a standalone readthrough agent to enable direct comparison of variant-specific 332 
efficacy, future studies could evaluate the combination of ELX-02 or follow-up readthrough 333 
molecules with CFTR modulators, as these may further rescue the function of readthrough-334 
generated CFTR protein increasing therapeutic benefit. 335 
Variability within genotypes was observed, consistent with previous work, possibly reflecting 336 
the heterogeneity in clinical responses among people with CF carrying identical CFTR 337 
variants treated with CFTR modulators, likely due to the influence of genetic modifiers and 338 
other patient-specific factors (8, 32).  339 
This work underlines the need for further improvements on small molecule-based readthrough 340 
strategies. Although combinatorial approaches could theoretically enhance rescue through 341 
corrector or potentiator mechanisms, prior work, including our own, indicates that ELX-02 342 
combined with ETI does not achieve sufficient functional rescue to expect clinical benefit 343 
(20). Future studies investigating whether the efficacy of ELX-02 can be further strengthened 344 
by newer and more effective modulators will be of interest, as will continued progress in the 345 
chemical optimization of readthrough compounds and the development of nonsense-mediated 346 
decay inhibitors. 347 
Despite limited ELX-02 efficacy, these findings underscore the need for informed patient 348 
selection when designing clinical trials for readthrough therapies, given the large 349 
heterogeneity in responses to readthrough compounds. PDIO-based functional screening 350 
suggests that not all nonsense variants respond equally, and that responses near the detection 351 
threshold can vary substantially. Ignoring this heterogeneity may dilute treatment effects and 352 
increase the risk of negative trial outcomes, even when a subset of patients could derive 353 
meaningful benefit in future clinical trials. Incorporating PDIO-based preclinical readouts into 354 
trial design enables rational prioritization of patients with more responsive nonsense variants, 355 
increasing the likelihood of detecting true clinical efficacy and supporting precise, 356 
mechanism-informed trial stratification, as recently demonstrated in the context of the 357 
CHOICES trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT064685270; EudraCT 2022-500410-26-01). In this 358 
context, systematic evaluation of novel therapeutic strategies across individual nonsense 359 
variants in a relevant preclinical model such as PDIOs is therefore essential. 360

(which was not certified by peer review) is the author/funder. All rights reserved. No reuse allowed without permission.

Figure 1 ELX-02 screening study design, CFTR nonsense variant distribution, genotype classification, and residual 
CFTR function. Schematic overview of the study design, including the number of included patients, the drug concentrations 
tested, the corresponding FIS assays performed, and the laboratories that conducted the screens (1A). Visualisation of the CFTR 
gene with the position of included nonsense variants, along with the corresponding CFTR primary protein structure  (1B). 
Classification of genotypes into predefined categories used for all subsequent analyses. Variants were categorized as minimal-
function (MF) variants when listed as such in the VX18-445-106 study protocol (Study-VX18-445-106-Eligible-Mutations-
June-2019.pdf) (1C). Waterfall plot of residual CFTR function measured by the FIS assay (2-hour swelling with medium only) 
for subjects according to genotype categories (1D). Violin plot of residual function  across the three genotype groups (1E). 
Biorender was used in the generation of Figure 1A.

Figure 2 Genotype-dependent response to ELX-02 in PDIOs primary screen. Waterfall plot for residual function-corrected 
0.8 µM forskolin FIS responses to ELX-02 at 80 µM for PDIOs harboring two nonsense variants (2A) and for PDIOs harboring 
one nonsense variant and one minimal function variant (2B). Three benchmarks are included: 1. Mean ELX-02 80 µM residual 
function-corrected FIS response of G542X/G542X PDIO reference line at 0.8 µM forskolin indicated in red (1384 AUC); 2. 
Mean lumacaftor/ivacaftor ( LUM/IV A) residual function-corrected FIS response of F508del/F508del PDIO reference line at 
0.8 µM forskolin indicated in green ( 4187 AUC); 3. Mean elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (E TI) residual function-corrected 
FIS response of F508del/F508del PDIO reference line at 0.8 µM forskolin indicated in green (9052 AUC). Error bars represent 
SEM (n = 2).  Only PDIOS with ELX -02 corrected responses above  the mean G542X/G542X ELX-02 at 80 µM response 
(1384 AUC) were included in both 2A and 2B gr aph. Responses below this benchmark are considered not clinically relevant 
and are not shown in the figure. Violin plot of the three categories across the two conditions used in the primary screen (ELX-
02 160 µM residual-function corrected, ELX-02 80 µM residual function-corrected) (2C). Violin plot of all genotypes with 
more than one PDIOs in the screen (mean AUC FIS ELX-02 80 µM) (2D). Violin plot of residual function-corrected swelling 
induced by ELX-02 at 80 and 160 µM according to type of premature termination codon (PTC) in PDIOs with one nonsense 
and one minimal function variant or two nonsense variants with the same type of PTC (2E).
